fields.h1: The Secret of Guidance by F. B. Meyer: Summary and Study Guide
fields.meta_title: The Secret of Guidance by F. B. Meyer: Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A study guide to F. B. Meyer’s The Secret of Guidance — how to know the will of God, its themes of the surrendered will and the Spirit-filled life, and how to read it.
fields.body_html:
If you have ever knelt at a crossroads and asked, in plain words, “Lord, which way?” then The Secret of Guidance was written for you. F. B. Meyer’s little classic, first published in 1896, sets out to answer one of the most practical questions in the Christian life: how can an ordinary believer know the will of God and walk in it with peace? Meyer’s answer is not a formula but a settled confidence — that a Father who loves his children will not leave them to guess. This study guide summarizes what the book teaches, how it is arranged, the themes to watch for, and how to read it today. Because Ochorus hosts the full text for free, you can move straight from this overview into Meyer’s own words.

What the book is, and Meyer’s aim

Meyer wrote as a pastor who had watched sincere Christians tie themselves in knots over decisions — career, marriage, calling, a move, a ministry — convinced that God had a path for them yet terrified of missing it. His aim is to steady such souls. The subject matters enormously, he insists, because so much of our usefulness depends on being in the place God has appointed:

The importance of the subject cannot be exaggerated; so much of our power and peace consists in knowing where God would have us be, and in being just there.

F. B. Meyer

The book’s premise is that God genuinely promises to guide, and that his promises can be trusted at face value. Meyer marshals them one after another — “I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go” (Psalm 32:8), “In all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct thy paths” (Proverbs 3:6), “The Lord shall guide thee continually” (Isaiah 58:11), and Christ’s own pledge, “I am the light of the world; he that followeth Me shall not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). Guidance, in other words, is not a rare privilege for spiritual giants but the ordinary birthright of anyone willing to trust and obey. Meyer’s deeper aim, though, is not merely to solve a decision but to lead the reader into the kind of surrendered, Spirit-filled life in which guidance becomes almost natural — the fruit of a heart already yielded to God.

How the book is organized

Despite its title, the book is not a single treatise but a gathering of nine short devotional chapters, each able to stand on its own yet all circling the same centre. It opens with the title chapter, “The Secret of Guidance,” which lays out Meyer’s core teaching on knowing God’s will. From there it broadens into the inner conditions that make guidance possible: “Where Am I Wrong?” searches out the hidden disobedience that blocks the light; “The Secret of Christ’s Indwelling” turns to the presence of Christ within the believer; and “Fact! Faith! Feeling!” corrects the emotional confusion that derails so many earnest seekers.

The later chapters apply the same restful trust to the whole of life. “Why Sign the Pledge?” treats decisive commitment; “Burdens, and What to Do with Them” and “How to Bear Sorrow” bring guidance to bear on anxiety and grief; “In the Secret of His Presence” dwells on communion with God; and the closing chapter, “The Fulness of the Spirit,” gathers everything into the pursuit Meyer cared about most — being filled with the Holy Spirit. The movement of the book is therefore from the question of guidance outward into a complete vision of the deeper Christian life.

The central themes

Discerning God’s guidance

Meyer’s most quoted teaching is his test for knowing God’s will. God does not, he says, guide us by a single channel that might mislead, but by the agreement of several. The inward prompting of the Spirit, the counsel of Scripture, and the shaping of outward circumstances converge like witnesses in a court:

The circumstances of our daily life are to us an infallible indication of God’s will, when they concur with the inward promptings of the Spirit and with the Word of God.

F. B. Meyer

Where the three do not yet agree, Meyer’s counsel is unhurried and freeing: “If you do not know what you ought to do, stand still until you do.” This is guidance for the anxious — a promise that the God who leads will also wait for the slow of heart, and that a willingness to be shown is itself half the answer (James 1:5). Meyer is candid, too, about the reasons the light seems withheld. Sometimes we cannot read God’s will because our own wishes shout too loudly; sometimes we are looking for a dramatic sign when God means to lead us step by ordinary step. His picture is of circumstances opening quietly, like glow-worms sparkling along a path, growing brighter and more numerous as we move in the right direction. The point is not to force a door but to keep close enough to God that we recognize the one he opens.

The surrendered will

Beneath the mechanics of discernment lies Meyer’s real concern: the state of the will. Most of our confusion, he argues, is not intellectual but moral — we cannot see the way because we are not yet willing to take it. The remedy is to move our life’s centre of gravity out of shifting emotion and into a will wholly given to God:

Let us, therefore, not live in the summer‑house of emotion, but in the central citadel of the will, wholly yielded and devoted to the will of God.

F. B. Meyer

This is the same note struck by Andrew Murray in Absolute Surrender, and it is the hinge of Meyer’s whole message: guidance flows to the surrendered, because the surrendered heart has stopped arguing and is ready to obey the moment the light appears (Proverbs 3:5).

Fact, faith, and feeling

A recurring danger Meyer names is the tyranny of feeling. Believers wait for a rush of emotion to confirm that God has spoken, and grow despondent when none comes. Meyer overturns the order. Feeling must never lead; it comes last, if it comes at all:

God’s Facts, laid like a foundation of adamant. Our Faith, apprehending and resting on them. Joyous Feelings, coming, it may be at once, or after the lapse of days and months, as God will.

F. B. Meyer

To rest on the fact of God’s love and finished work, whether or not the heart feels it, is for Meyer the secret of steadiness. He compares the facts of Scripture to stepping-stones across a brook: you cannot judge them from the bank, but once you step down and put your weight on them you find they hold. Even our burdens are meant to be handed over rather than carried, according to the promise, “Cast thy burden upon the Lord, and He shall sustain thee” (Psalm 55:22), so that the peace of God that passes understanding may keep the heart (Philippians 4:7). Care, Meyer warns, breaks the soul’s rest as surely as sin does, and the cure is the same in both cases — to bring the load to God and leave it there.

The deeper, Spirit-filled life

Finally, Meyer sees guidance as one blessing among many that belong to the believer indwelt and filled by the Holy Spirit. His great phrase for the Christian secret is the mystery Paul unveiled — “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27) — and his closing summons is to be “filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18) as the settled, normal condition of the soul. Guidance, comfort in sorrow, victory over care, and joyful communion are not separate techniques but the natural overflow of a life in which Christ has been given full room.

Who should read it

This is a book for anyone facing a decision and longing to get it right — students weighing a calling, workers considering a change, believers sensing a nudge toward some new step and afraid of presumption. It is equally for the anxious Christian whose faith rides on feelings, and for the grieving and burdened who need to learn how to lay their loads down. Because Meyer writes for the timid rather than the confident, stooping to the “dullest child who truly wants to obey,” it suits new believers as readily as seasoned ones. Pastors and mentors will recognize in it a gentle counterweight to the two errors they see most often — the paralysis that will not act without certainty, and the presumption that mistakes emotion for the voice of God. Small groups will find its short, self-contained chapters easy to discuss, and its brevity means a thoughtful reader can finish it in a couple of unhurried sittings, then return to single chapters as need arises.

How to read it today

Read it slowly, and read it as a participant rather than a spectator. Meyer means his counsel to be obeyed, not merely admired, so pause at the end of each chapter to ask where its teaching touches your own life. When you reach the guidance test, try it on a real decision you are carrying: name the inward prompting, search the Scriptures, and watch the circumstances — then, if they do not yet agree, take Meyer at his word and wait. His nineteenth-century English is warm and vivid but occasionally ornate; let the images carry you rather than slowing over every phrase. Keep a Bible open, since Meyer reasons straight from the promises, and keep the surrendered will in view as the thread that ties every chapter together. You can read the complete book free on Ochorus, written by F. B. Meyer, and pair it with his companion deeper-life classic The Way Into the Holiest or with Hannah Whitall Smith’s The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life, which sounds the same call to surrender and trust.

For reflection

  1. Meyer says our “power and peace” depend on being exactly where God wants us. Where in your life are you unsure whether you are in that place — and what would it take to find out?
  2. Apply Meyer’s threefold test to a decision you are facing now. What is the inward prompting of the Spirit, what does the Word of God say, and how are your circumstances moving? Where do they agree, and where must you still wait?
  3. Are you living in “the summer‑house of emotion” or “the central citadel of the will”? Is there a point where your will is quietly refusing what you already know God asks?
  4. Meyer orders the Christian life as fact, then faith, then feeling. Where have you reversed that order, waiting for a feeling before you would trust a promise?
  5. What burden are you carrying that Meyer would tell you to cast on the Lord — and what has kept you from letting it go?
